content: Palmar Plantar Erythrodysesthesia (PPE), also known as Hand-Foot Syndrome, is a dermatologic condition primarily affecting the palms and soles. It is most commonly associated with the use of certain chemotherapeutic agents in cancer treatment. The condition is characterized by a range of symptoms, including erythema, swelling, pain, and desquamation of the affected areas. PPE is classified into four grades based on the severity of symptoms, ranging from mild to severe. The pathophysiology of PPE remains under investigation, but several mechanisms have been proposed. One key factor is the deposition of chemotherapeutic agents, such as pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD), into the eccrine sweat glands, which are highly concentrated in the palms and soles. The drug is excreted in sweat, leading to its accumulation in the stratum corneum, the thick outermost layer of the skin. This accumulation acts as a reservoir for the drug, resulting in a toxic reaction and the clinical manifestations of PPE. Other contributing factors include rapid cell turnover in the skin of the palms and soles, vascular anatomy, gravitational forces, and temperature gradients in the distal extremities. Histopathological examination of PPE lesions reveals nonspecific findings consistent with a toxic reaction. These include vacuolar degeneration of the basal cell layer, mild spongiosis, keratinocyte necrosis, papillary dermal edema, lymphocytic infiltrates, and partial separation of the epidermis from the dermis. Additional findings may include perivascular infiltrates composed of eosinophils and lymphocytes, as well as eccrine squamous syringometaplasia or neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis. Some evidence suggests that small-fiber neuropathy may contribute to the pain and dysesthesia experienced by patients. PPE is most frequently associated with chemotherapeutic agents such as pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, 5-fluorouracil, cytarabine, methotrexate (even at low doses), mitotane, docetaxel, capecitabine, vinorelbine, gemcitabine, and sorafenib. Additional predictors include the use of cooling mechanisms, a higher number of PLD cycles, and the presence of mucositis, neutropenia, or peripheral neuropathy. The clinical presentation of PPE typically begins with a sensation of tingling or numbness in the palms and soles. This progresses to painful, well-demarcated swelling and erythematous plaques, which are often symmetric. In the resolution phase, desquamation of the affected areas occurs. A rare but documented complication of PPE is the loss of fingerprints, as seen in a patient treated with capecitabine. Differentiating PPE from other conditions is essential for accurate diagnosis and management. For example, PPE must be distinguished from Tinea manuum, which responds to antifungal therapy, and from acute graft-versus-host disease, which typically involves other areas of the body. PPE can also mimic hand-foot skin reactions caused by tyrosine kinase inhibitors, but these conditions can be differentiated based on clinical features. PPE presents with diffuse erythema due to a cytotoxic reaction, whereas hand-foot skin reactions are characterized by focal hyperkeratotic lesions. Management of PPE includes both preventive and therapeutic strategies. For example, reducing the dose intensity of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin to less than 10 mg/m² weekly has been shown to effectively prevent PPE. Supportive care, such as the use of emollients and pain management, is essential for improving patient quality of life. In summary, Palmar Plantar Erythrodysesthesia is a chemotherapy-induced dermatologic condition with a well-defined clinical presentation and histopathological features. While its pathophysiology is not fully understood, advances in research have provided insights into its mechanisms and risk factors.
